source_text: 8.8 Ἁπλῶς ἀναγινωσκόμενα τὰ ῥήματα τῆς Γραφῆς, συλλαβαί τινες εἰσι μικραί· Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ· ἐρευνωμένης δὲ τῆς ἐν τοῖς ῥήμασι διανοίας, τότε ἐκφαίνεται τὸ μέγα θαῦμα τῆς σοφίας τοῦ κτίσαντος. Πόσας προείδετο διαφορὰς πτηνῶν; ὅπως αὐτὰ κατὰ γένος διέστησεν ἀπ' ἀλλήλων; πῶς ἕκαστον κεχωρισμένοις ἐχαρακτήρισεν ἰδιώ μασιν; Ἐπιλείπει με ἡ ἡμέρα, τὰ ἐναέρια ὑμῖν θαύματα διηγούμενον. Καλεῖ ἡμᾶς ἡ χέρσος πρὸς τὴν τῶν θηρίων καὶ ἑρπετῶν καὶ βοσκημάτων ἐπίδειξιν, ἑτοίμως ἔχουσα ὁμότιμα τοῖς φυτοῖς καὶ τῷ πλωτῷ γένει καὶ τοῖς πτηνοῖς πᾶσιν ἀντεπιδείξασθαι. Ἐξαγαγέτω ἡ γῆ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν κτηνῶν καὶ θηρίων καὶ ἑρπετῶν κατὰ γένος. Τί φατε, οἱ ἀπιστοῦντες τῷ Παύλῳ περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἀλλοιώσεως, ὁρῶντες πολλὰ τῶν ἀερίων τὰς μορφὰς μεταβάλ λοντα; Ὁποῖα καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰνδικοῦ σκώληκος ἱστορεῖται τοῦ κερασφόρου· ὃς εἰς κάμπην τὰ πρῶτα μεταβαλὼν, εἶτα προϊὼν βομβυλιὸς γίνεται, καὶ οὐδὲ ἐπὶ ταύτης ἵσταται τῆς μορφῆς, ἀλλὰ χαύνοις καὶ πλατέσι πετάλοις ὑποπτεροῦται. Ὅταν οὖν καθέζησθε τὴν τούτων ἐργασίαν ἀναπηνιζόμεναι, αἱ γυναῖκες, τὰ νήματα λέγω ἃ πέμπουσιν ὑμῖν οἱ Σῆρες πρὸς τὴν τῶν μαλακῶν ἐνδυμάτων κατασκευὴν, μεμνημέναι τῆς κατὰ τὸ ζῷον τοῦτο μεταβολῆς, ἐναργῆ λαμβάνετε τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἔννοιαν, καὶ μὴ ἀπιστεῖτε τῇ ἀλλαγῇ ἣν Παῦλος ἅπασι κατεπαγγέλλεται. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ αἰσθάνομαι τοῦ λόγου τὴν συμμετρίαν ἐκβαίνοντος. Ὅταν μὲν οὖν ἀπίδω πρὸς τὸ πλῆθος τῶν εἰρημένων, ἔξω ἐμαυτὸν ὁρῶ τοῦ μέτρου φερόμενον· ὅταν δὲ πάλιν πρὸς τὸ ποικίλον τῆς ἐν τοῖς δημιουργήμασι σοφίας ἀποβλέψω, οὐδὲ ἦρχθαι νομίζω τῆς διηγήσεως. Ἅμα δὲ καὶ τὸ παρακατέχειν ὑμᾶς ἐπὶ πλεῖον οὐκ ἄχρηστον. Τί γὰρ ἄν τις καὶ ποιοῖ τὸν μέχρι τῆς ἑσπέρας χρόνον; Οὐκ ἐπείγουσιν ὑμᾶς οἱ ἑστιάτορες· οὐκ ἀναμένει ὑμᾶς τὰ συμπόσια. Ὅθεν, εἰ δοκεῖ, τῇ σωματικῇ νηστείᾳ εἰς τὴν τῶν ψυχῶν εὐφροσύνην ἀποχρησώμεθα. Πολλάκις ὑπηρετήσας τῇ σαρκὶ πρὸς ἀπόλαυσιν, σήμερον τῇ διακονίᾳ παράμεινον τῆς ψυχῆς. Κατατρύφησον τοῦ Κυρίου, καὶ δώσει σοι τὰ αἰτήματα τῆς καρδίας σου. Εἰ φιλόπλουτος εἶ, ἔχεις πλοῦτον πνευματικὸν, Τὰ κρίματα Κυρίου τὰ ἀληθινὰ, τὰ δεδικαιωμένα ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, τὰ ἐπιθυμητὰ ὑπὲρ χρυσίον καὶ λίθον τίμιον πολύν. Εἰ ἀπολαυστικὸς καὶ φιλήδονος, ἔχεις τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ τῷ τὴν πνευματικὴν αἴσθησιν ἐρρωμένῳ Γλυκύτερα ὄντα ὑπὲρ μέλι καὶ κηρίον. Ἐὰν ὑμᾶς διαφῶ, καὶ διαλύσω τὸν σύλλογον, οἱ μὲν ἐπὶ τοὺς κύβους δραμοῦνται. Ὅρκοι ἐκεῖ, καὶ φιλονεικίαι χαλεπαὶ, καὶ φιλοχρηματίας ὠδῖνες. Δαίμων παρέστηκε διὰ τῶν κατεστιγμένων ὀστέων τὴν μανίαν ἐξάπτων, καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ χρήματα πρὸς ἑκάτερον μέρος μετατιθεὶς, νῦν τοῦτον ἐπαίρων τῇ νίκῃ, κἀκείνῳ κατήφειαν ἐμποιῶν, πάλιν δὲ ἐκεῖνον γαυριῶντα δεικνὺς, καὶ τοῦτον κατῃσχυμμένον. Τί ὄφελος, νηστεύειν τῷ σώματι, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν μυρίων κακῶν ἐμπεπλῆσθαι; Ὁ μὴ κυβεύων, σχολὴν δὲ ἄλλως ἄγων, τί οὐ φθέγγεται τῶν ματαίων; τί οὐκ ἀκούει τῶν ἀτόπων; Σχολὴ γὰρ, ἄνευ φόβου Θεοῦ, πονηρίας διδάσκαλος τοῖς ἀκαιρουμένοις ἐστί. Τάχα μὲν οὖν τι καὶ ὄφελος ἐν τοῖς λεγομένοις εὑρήσεται· εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἀλλὰ τό γε μὴ ἁμαρτάνειν ἐκ τῆς ἐνταῦθα ὑμῖν ἀσχολίας περίεστιν.
thought_title: The wonder of winged creatures and the profit of staying
orientation: Basil is preaching on the fifth day's creation of birds and water creatures, and now turns to the wonder of winged creatures, then urges his hearers to stay for spiritual nourishment rather than idle pursuits.
pass_a_gloss: Simply read, the words of Scripture are some small syllables: 'Let the waters bring forth winged creatures flying upon the earth along the firmament of heaven'; but when the thought in the words is searched out, then the great wonder of the wisdom of the Creator is revealed. How many differences of winged creatures did he foresee? How did he separate them from one another according to kind? How did he mark each one with distinct peculiarities? The day fails me as I recount to you the wonders of the air. The dry land calls us to the display of wild beasts and creeping things and cattle, being ready to show in return things of equal honor to the plants and to the swimming kind and to all the winged creatures. 'Let the earth bring forth living creature of cattle and wild beasts and creeping things according to kind.' What do you say, you who disbelieve Paul concerning the change at the resurrection, when you see many of the creatures of the air changing their forms? Such things are also reported about the Indian horned worm: which first changes into a caterpillar, then as it advances becomes a bombylius, and does not even stop at this form, but is winged beneath with loose and broad leaves. Whenever therefore you sit unwinding the work of these, O women—I mean the threads which the Chinese send you for the making of soft garments—remembering the change of this creature, take a clear notion of the resurrection, and do not disbelieve the change which Paul proclaims to all. But indeed I perceive that the discourse is going beyond its proper measure. Whenever therefore I look to the multitude of things said, I see myself carried outside the measure; but whenever again I look to the varied wisdom in the created works, I think I have not even begun the narration. And at the same time, keeping you here longer is not without profit. For what would anyone do with the time until evening? The hosts do not press you; the drinking parties do not await you. Therefore, if it seems good, let us use the bodily fast for the gladness of souls. Having often served the flesh for enjoyment, today remain in the service of the soul. Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart. If you are a lover of wealth, you have spiritual wealth: the judgments of the Lord, the true ones, justified altogether, desirable beyond gold and much precious stone. If you are a lover of enjoyment and pleasure, you have the oracles of God, which to the one strong in spiritual perception are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. If I dismiss you and dissolve the assembly, some will run to the dice. Oaths there, and harsh quarrels, and pangs of love of money. A demon stands by, kindling madness through the marked bones, and moving the same money to each side, now lifting this one up by victory, and producing dejection in that one, and again showing that one exulting and this one put to shame. What profit is it to fast in the body, but to have the soul filled with ten thousand evils? The one who does not play dice, but otherwise passes leisure, what vain things does he not utter? What absurd things does he not hear? For leisure, without fear of God, is a teacher of wickedness to those who are unseasonable. Perhaps then some profit will be found in the things said; but if not, at least the not sinning from your occupation here is a gain.

pass_b_english: Read simply, the words of Scripture are only small syllables: “Let the waters bring forth winged creatures flying upon the earth along the firmament of heaven” (Genesis 1:20). But when the meaning within the words is searched out, then the great wonder of the Creator’s wisdom is revealed. How many varieties of birds did he foresee? How did he separate them from one another according to kind? How did he mark each one with distinct characteristics? The day fails me as I describe to you the wonders of the air. The dry land calls us to the display of wild beasts, reptiles, and cattle, ready to show in return creatures equal in honor to the plants, the swimming kind, and all the birds. “Let the earth bring forth the living creature of cattle and wild beasts and reptiles according to kind” (Genesis 1:24). What do you say, you who disbelieve Paul about the change at the resurrection, when you see many of the creatures of the air changing their forms? Such is the story told about the horned Indian worm: it first changes into a caterpillar, then as it advances becomes a chrysalis, and it does not stop at this form, but is furnished with wings of loose and broad leaf-like scales. So when you women sit unwinding the work of these creatures—I mean the threads the Chinese send you for the making of soft garments—remember the change of this animal, and receive a vivid conception of the resurrection, and do not disbelieve the change that Paul proclaims to all. But I sense that my discourse is going beyond its proper measure. When I look at the abundance of what has been said, I see myself carried beyond the limit; but when I look again at the variety of wisdom in the created works, I think I have not even begun the account. And at the same time, keeping you here longer is not without benefit. For what would one do with the time until evening? No hosts are pressing you; no banquets await you. Therefore, if it seems good, let us use the bodily fast for the gladness of our souls. You have often served the flesh for enjoyment; today remain in the service of the soul. Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart (Psalm 36:4 LXX). If you love wealth, you have spiritual wealth: the judgments of the Lord, the true ones, justified altogether, desirable beyond gold and much precious stone (Psalm 18:10-11 LXX [Hebrew 19:9-10]). If you love enjoyment and pleasure, you have the words of God, which to the one strong in spiritual perception are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Psalm 18:11 LXX [Hebrew 19:10]). If I dismiss you and dissolve the assembly, some will run to the dice. There are oaths, harsh quarrels, and the pangs of greed. A demon stands by, kindling madness through the marked bones, shifting the same money to one side or the other—now lifting this one up with victory and filling that one with gloom, then showing that one exulting and this one put to shame. What profit is there in fasting in the body while the soul is filled with countless evils? The one who does not gamble but passes his leisure otherwise—what vain things does he not utter? What absurd things does he not hear? For leisure without the fear of God is a teacher of wickedness to those who use their time badly. Perhaps, then, some benefit will be found in what has been said; but if not, at least the avoidance of sin comes to you from your occupation here.

problems.quote: is winged underneath with loose and broad leaf-like structures
problems.why: English 'winged underneath' for ὑποπτεροῦται. The verb means 'is furnished with wings beneath' or 'has wings underneath.' But πετάλοις means 'leaves' or 'petals,' here 'wing-covers' or 'scales.' The silkworm moth has wings beneath the loose broad scales/leaf-like structures. The English 'winged underneath with' suggests the wings are underneath the leaf-like structures, but the Greek says it is winged/furnished with wings by means of or characterized by loose broad leaf-like structures (scales). The syntax is ὑποπτεροῦται χαύνοις καὶ πλατέσι πετάλοις—'is winged with loose and broad leaf-like structures.' The English 'underneath' misreads ὑπο- as 'underneath' rather than as part of ὑποπτεροῦται 'to wing, furnish with wings.' This changes the physical description.
problems.fix: is furnished with wings of loose and broad leaf-like scales

fixed: The English 'winged underneath' misreads the Greek verb ὑποπτεροῦται, which means 'is furnished with wings' (ὑπο- is part of the verb, not 'underneath'). The dative πετάλοις describes the wings as loose and broad leaf-like scales. Changed to 'is furnished with wings of loose and broad leaf-like scales.'

dismissed.why: βομβυλίος means silkworm/moth, not chrysalis; the next stage is winged moth.
dismissed.note: Here βομβυλιός is the cocoon stage (as in Aristotle HA 551b), before the winged form, so 'chrysalis' is fair.
